title: Violence at Home and Suicide Risk in Young Women: A Cross-Country Analysis From Chile,  Spain and Mexico
content: Suicide is a leading cause of death among young women, yet the interplay between domestic vio-lence and suicide risk across different sociocultural contexts remains under-researched. Grounded in the Social-Ecological Model, this study examines how perceived household violence associates with suicide risk severity among young women in Spain, Chile, and Mexico. A cross-sectional study using smartphone-based screening collected data from 15,526 women aged 15–24 in Chile, Spain, and Mexico was conducted. Suicide risk severity was analyzed with multivariable ordinal and binary logistic regression, adjusting for perceived household violence, depressive symptoms, anxi-ety, psychological well-being, substance use, non-suicidal self-injury, age, and country. Perceived household violence was independently associated with higher suicide risk, even after adjusting for mental health and behavioral factors. Depressive symptoms had the strongest association; anxiety, lower well-being, drug use, hazardous alcohol consumption, and prior self-injury were also asso-ciated. Younger age increased risk, while country of residence was not independently associated. Household violence is a key factor in suicide risk among young women. Prevention strategies should integrate multilevel, context-sensitive interventions addressing both mental health and family environments.
